otherwise provided for.—Whoever, being a public servant legally bound as such public servant to
apprehend, or to keep in confinement, any person in any case not provided for in section 259, section 260

question: How does Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code (Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
expanded: How does Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code (Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
answer:
**Direct Answer** Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 237 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) are **identical in their operative wording**. Both criminalise the corrupt use or attempted use of a declaration known to be false in any material point, prescribing the same punishment as for giving false evidence. The only difference lies in the cross‑references within their respective Explanations, reflecting the renumbering of provisions in the BNS. --- **Statutory Text** | Provision | Text | |-----------|------| | **IPC Section 200** [Source 2] | “Whoever corruptly uses or attempts to use as true any such declaration, knowing the same to be false in any material point, shall be punished in the same manner as if he gave false evidence.”

**Explanation.** — “A declaration which is inadmissible merely upon the ground of some informality, is a declaration within the meaning of sections 199 and 200.” | | **BNS Section 237** [Source 1] | “Whoever corruptly uses or attempts to use as true any such declaration, knowing the same to be false in any material point, shall be punished in the same manner as if he gave false evidence.”

**Explanation.** — “A declaration which is inadmissible merely upon the ground of some informality, is a declaration within the meaning of section 236 and this section.” | --- **Key Differences** 1. **Cross‑reference in the Explanation** - IPC Section 200 refers to “sections 199 and 200” (the false‑declaration offence and the present section). - BNS Section 237 refers to “section 236 and this section” (the corresponding false‑declaration offence in BNS and the present section). This change is purely consequential to the re‑numbering of the chapter; the substantive scope of “declaration” remains the same. 2. **Section Numbers** - IPC: Section 200 (Chapter XI). - BNS: Section 237 (Chapter XIV). 3. **No Change in Punishment or Elements** Both provisions impose punishment “in the same manner as if he gave false evidence” and require the same mental element (“knowing the same to be false in any material point”) and actus reus (“corruptly uses or attempts to use as true”). --- **Practical Implications** - **Continuity of Law**: Practitioners can treat the two provisions as functionally equivalent; case law under IPC Section 200 will remain directly applicable to BNS Section 237. - **Drafting and Pleading**: Only the section number and the cross‑reference in the Explanation need updating in legal documents. - **Interpretation of “Declaration”**: The definition of “declaration” (including informally defective declarations) is preserved verbatim, with the BNS pointing to its own Section 236 [Source 5] instead of IPC Sections 199/200.

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIII - OF CONTEMPTS OF THE LAWFUL AUTHORITY OF PUBLIC SERVANTS | Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of another person
217. False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of
another person—Whoever gives to any public servant any information which he knows or believes to be
false, intending thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, such public
servant—
(a) to do or omit anything which such public servant ought not to do or omit if the true state of
facts respecting which such information is given were known by him; or
(b) to use the lawful power of such public servant to the injury or annoyance of any person,
shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or
with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.
(a) A informs a Magistrate that Z, a police officer, subordinate to such Magistrate, has been
guilty of neglect of duty or misconduct, knowing such information to be false, and knowing it to be
likely that the information will cause the Magistrate to dismiss Z. A has committed the offence
defined in this section.
(b) A falsely informs a public servant that Z has contraband salt in a secret place, knowing such
information to be false, and knowing that it is likely that the consequence of the information will be a
search of Z’s premises, attended with annoyance to Z. A has committed the offence defined in this
section.
(c) A falsely informs a policeman that he has been assaulted and robbed in the neighbourhood of
a particular village. He does not mention the name of any person as one of his assailants, but knows it
to be likely that in consequence of this information the police will make enquiries and institute
searches in the village to the annoyance of the villagers or some of them. A has committed an offence
under this section.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIII - OF CONTEMPTS OF THE LAWFUL AUTHORITY OF PUBLIC SERVANTS | Section 212: Furnishing false information
212. Furnishing false information.—Whoever, being legally bound to furnish information on any
subject to any public servant, as such, furnishes, as true, information on the subject which he knows or
has reason to believe to be false,—
(a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or
with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both;
(b) where the information which he is legally bound to give respects the commission of an
offence, or is required for the purpose of preventing the commission of an offence, or in order to the
apprehension of an offender, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to
two years, or with fine, or with both.
(a) A, a landholder, knowing of the commission of a murder within the limits of his estate,
wilfully misinforms the Magistrate of the district that the death has occurred by accident in
consequence of the bite of a snake. A is guilty of the offence defined in this section.
(b) A, a village watchman, knowing that a considerable body of strangers has passed through his
village in order to commit a dacoity in the house of Z, a wealthy merchant residing in a neighbouring
place, and being legally bound to give early and punctual information of the above fact to the officer
of the nearest police station, wilfully misinforms the police officer that a body of suspicious
characters passed through the village with a view to commit dacoity in a certain distant place in a
different direction. Here A is guilty of the offence defined in this section.
Explanation.—In section 211 and in this section the word “offence” include any act committed at any
place out of India, which, if committed in India, would be punishable under any of the following sections,
namely, 103, 105, 307, sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 309, sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and (5) of
section 310, 311, 312, clauses (f) and (g) of section 326, sub-sections (4), (6), (7) and (8) of section 331,
clauses (a) and (b) of section 332 and the word “offender” includes any person who is alleged to have
been guilty of any such act.

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIV - OF FALSE EVIDENCE AND OFFENCES AGAINST PUBLIC JUSTICE | Section 227: Giving false evidence
227. Giving false evidence.—Whoever, being legally bound by an oath or by an express provision of
law to state the truth, or being bound by law to make a declaration upon any subject, makes any statement
which is false, and which he either knows or believes to be false or does not believe to be true, is said to
give false evidence.
Explanation 1.—A statement is within the meaning of this section, whether it is made verbally or
otherwise.
Explanation 2.—A false statement as to the belief of the person attesting is within the meaning of this
section, and a person may be guilty of giving false evidence by stating that he believes a thing which he
does not believe, as well as by stating that he knows a thing which he does not know.
(a) A, in support of a just claim which B has against Z for one thousand rupees, falsely swears on a
trial that he heard Z admit the justice of B’s claim. A has given false evidence.
(b) A, being bound by an oath to state the truth, states that he believes a certain signature to be the
handwriting of Z, when he does not believe it to be the handwriting of Z. Here A states that which he
knows to be false, and therefore gives false evidence.
(c) A, knowing the general character of Z’s handwriting, states that he believes a certain signature to
be the handwriting of Z; A in good faith believing it to be so. Here A’s statement is merely as to his
belief, and is true as to his belief, and therefore, although the signature may not be the handwriting of Z,
A has not given false evidence.
(d) A, being bound by an oath to state the truth, states that he knows that Z was at a particular place
on a particular day, not knowing anything upon the subject. A gives false evidence whether Z was at that
place on the day named or not.
(e) A, an interpreter or translator, gives or certifies as a true interpretation or translation of a
statement or document which he is bound by oath to interpret or translate truly, that which is not and
which he does not believe to be a true interpretation or translation. A has given false evidence.

**Direct Answer** Section 200 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 237 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) are **identical in their operative wording**. Both criminalise the corrupt use or attempted use of a declaration known to be false in any material point, prescribing the same punishment as for giving false evidence. The only difference lies in the cross‑references within their respective Explanations, reflecting the renumbering of provisions in the BNS. --- **Statutory Text** | Provision | Text | |-----------|------| | **IPC Section 200** [Source 2] | “Whoever corruptly uses or attempts to use as true any such declaration, knowing the same to be false in any material point, shall be punished in the same manner as if he gave false evidence.”

**Explanation.** — “A declaration which is inadmissible merely upon the ground of some informality, is a declaration within the meaning of sections 199 and 200.” | | **BNS Section 237** [Source 1] | “Whoever corruptly uses or attempts to use as true any such declaration, knowing the same to be false in any material point, shall be punished in the same manner as if he gave false evidence.”

**Explanation.** — “A declaration which is inadmissible merely upon the ground of some informality, is a declaration within the meaning of section 236 and this section.” | --- **Key Differences** 1. **Cross‑reference in the Explanation** - IPC Section 200 refers to “sections 199 and 200” (the false‑declaration offence and the present section). - BNS Section 237 refers to “section 236 and this section” (the corresponding false‑declaration offence in BNS and the present section). This change is purely consequential to the re‑numbering of the chapter; the substantive scope of “declaration” remains the same. 2. **Section Numbers** - IPC: Section 200 (Chapter XI). - BNS: Section 237 (Chapter XIV). 3. **No Change in Punishment or Elements** Both provisions impose punishment “in the same manner as if he gave false evidence” and require the same mental element (“knowing the same to be false in any material point”) and actus reus (“corruptly uses or attempts to use as true”). --- **Practical Implications** - **Continuity of Law**: Practitioners can treat the two provisions as functionally equivalent; case law under IPC Section 200 will remain directly applicable to BNS Section 237. - **Drafting and Pleading**: Only the section number and the cross‑reference in the Explanation need updating in legal documents. - **Interpretation of “Declaration”**: The definition of “declaration” (including informally defective declarations) is preserved verbatim, with the BNS pointing to its own Section 236 [Source 5] instead of IPC Sections 199/200.

question: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 166 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Abetment of act of insubordination by soldier, sailor or airman)?
expanded: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 166 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Abetment of act of insubordination by soldier, sailor or airman)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
Section 138 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 is the predecessor of Section 166 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Both provisions share the identical title and core offence — abetment of an act of insubordination by a soldier, sailor or airman — but the maximum term of imprisonment has been increased from six months to two years.

**Statutory Text**

| Provision | Text (key elements) |
|-----------|---------------------|
| **IPC Section 138** | “Whoever abets what he knows to be an act of insubordination by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force, of the Government of India, shall, if such act of insubordination be committed in consequence of that abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.” [Source 2] |
| **BNS Section 166** | “Whoever abets what he knows to be an act of insubordination by an officer, soldier, sailor or airman, in the Army, Navy or Air Force, of the Government of India, shall, if such act of insubordination be committed in consequence of that abetment, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.” [Source 1] |

**Key Difference (IPC → BNS)**  
- **Maximum imprisonment:** increased from **six months** (IPC) to **two years** (BNS).  
- Fine and “both” alternatives remain unchanged.  
- Wording and structure are otherwise identical.

**Practical Implication**  
The enhanced maximum sentence under BNS Section 166 gives courts wider sentencing discretion for this military‑related abetment offence, reflecting a legislative intent to treat insubordination abetment more severely than under the IPC.

question: Compare Section 42 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (When such right extends to causing any harm other than death) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
expanded: Compare Section 42 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (When such right extends to causing any harm other than death) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
Section 42 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) corresponds to Section 104 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Both provisions govern the right of private defence of property when the offence is theft, mischief, or criminal trespass **not** falling within the more serious categories that justify causing death. The right extends to causing any harm **other than death**, subject to the general restrictions on private defence.

---

### Statutory Text Comparison

41. When right of private defence of property extends to causing death.—The right of private
defence of property extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of
death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting

person.—If in the exercise of the right of private defence against an assault which reasonably causes the
apprehension of death, the defender be so situated that he cannot effectually exercise that right without
risk of harm to an innocent person, his right of private defence extends to the running of that risk.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER III - GENERAL EXCEPTIONS | Section 29: Exclusion of acts which are offences independently of harm caused
29. Exclusion of acts which are offences independently of harm caused.—The exceptions in
sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they
may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or
on whose behalf the consent is given.
Causing miscarriage (unless caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman) is
an offence independently of any harm which it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman.
Therefore, it is not an offence “by reason of such harm”; and the consent of the woman or of her guardian
to the causing of such miscarriage does not justify the act.

question: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 394 of the Indian Penal Code (Voluntarily causing hurt in committing robbery)?
expanded: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 394 of the Indian Penal Code (Voluntarily causing hurt in committing robbery)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
The provision in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 that corresponds to IPC Section 394 (Voluntarily causing hurt in committing robbery) is **Section 309(6)** of the BNS.

---

**Statutory Text Comparison**

| Aspect | IPC Section 394 [Source 1] | BNS Section 309(6) [Source 2] |
|--------|----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Offence** | Voluntarily causing hurt in committing or attempting to commit robbery | Same: voluntarily causing hurt in committing or attempting to commit robbery |
| **Persons liable** | The offender and any other person jointly concerned | Same: the offender and any other person jointly concerned |
| **Punishment** | Imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine | Identical: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine |

---

**Key Observations**

1. **Structural difference** – In the IPC, the offence is a standalone section (Section 394). In the BNS, it is embedded as **sub-section (6) of Section 309**, which consolidates the definition, basic punishment, and aggravated forms of robbery in a single section.
2. **No substantive change** – The wording, scope of joint liability, and quantum of punishment are identical.
3. **Related aggravated provision** – BNS Section 311 [Source 3] prescribes a minimum 7‑year imprisonment when robbery/dacoity involves a deadly weapon, grievous hurt, or attempt to cause death/grievous hurt. This is a separate, higher‑threshold aggravation and does not replace Section 309(6).

---

**Practical Implication**  
Prosecutors and courts will now charge the offence under **BNS Section 309(6)** instead of IPC Section 394. The elements to prove, the range of punishment, and the principle of joint liability remain unchanged, so existing case law on IPC Section 394 continues to be directly applicable.

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY | Section 309: Robbery
309. Robbery.—(1) In all robbery there is either theft or extortion.
(2) Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in
carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end
voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant
death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.
(3) Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of
the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant
hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear,
induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.
Explanation.—The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in
fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.
(a) A holds Z down, and fraudulently takes Z’s money and jewels from Z’s clothes, without Z’s
consent. Here A has committed theft, and, in order to the committing of that theft, has voluntarily caused
wrongful restraint to Z. A has therefore committed robbery.
(b) A meets Z on the high road, shows a pistol, and demands Z’s purse. Z, in consequence, surrenders
his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z by putting him in fear of instant hurt, and being at the
time of committing the extortion in his presence. A has therefore committed robbery.
(c) A meets Z and Z’s child on the high road. A takes the child, and threatens to fling it down a
precipice, unless Z delivers his purse. Z, in consequence, delivers his purse. Here A has extorted the
purse from Z, by causing Z to be in fear of instant hurt to the child who is there present. A has therefore
committed robbery on Z.
(d) A obtains property from Z by saying—“Your child is in the hands of my gang, and will be put to
death unless you send us ten thousand rupees”. This is extortion, and punishable as such; but it is not
robbery, unless Z is put in fear of the instant death of his child.
(4) Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may
extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway
between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.
(5) Whoever attempts to commit robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term
which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(6) If any person, in committing or in attempting to commit robbery, voluntarily causes hurt, such
person, and any other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting to commit such robbery, shall
be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to
ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER VI - OF OFFENCES AFFECTING THE HUMAN BODY | Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of property
120. Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of
property.—(1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt for the purpose of extorting from the sufferer or from
any person interested in the sufferer, any confession or any information which may lead to the detection
of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the sufferer or any person interested in the
sufferer to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim
or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security,
shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years,
and shall also be liable to fine.
(a) A, a police officer, tortures Z in order to induce Z to confess that he committed a crime. A is
guilty of an offence under this section.
(b) A, a police officer, tortures B to induce him to point out where certain stolen property is
deposited. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
(c) A, a revenue officer, tortures Z in order to compel him to pay certain arrears of revenue due from
Z. A is guilty of an offence under this section.
(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt for any purpose referred to in sub-section (1), shall be
punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also
be liable to fine.

person interested in the sufferer, any property or valuable security, or of constraining the sufferer or any
person interested in such sufferer to do anything which is illegal or which may facilitate the commission

115. Voluntarily causing hurt.—(1) Whoever does any act with the intention of thereby causing
hurt to any person, or with the knowledge that he is likely thereby to cause hurt to any person, and does
thereby cause hurt to any person, is said “voluntarily to cause hurt”.
(2) Whoever, except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122 voluntarily causes
hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year,
or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both.

118. Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means.—(1) Whoever,
except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122, voluntarily causes hurt by means of any
instrument for shooting, stabbing or cutting, or any instrument which, used as a weapon of offence, is
likely to cause death, or by means of fire or any heated substance, or by means of any poison or any

hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause hurt
to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of
either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five
thousand rupees, or with both.

nor knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt to any person other than the person who gave the

A instigates B to resist by force a distress made by a public servant. B, in consequence, resists that
distress. In offering the resistance, B voluntarily causes grievous hurt to the officer executing the distress.
As B has committed both the offence of resisting the distress, and the offence of voluntarily causing
grievous hurt, B is liable to punishment for both these offences; and, if A knew that B was likely

**Direct Answer:**  
The provision in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 that corresponds to IPC Section 394 (Voluntarily causing hurt in committing robbery) is **Section 309(6)** of the BNS.

---

**Statutory Text Comparison**

| Aspect | IPC Section 394 [Source 1] | BNS Section 309(6) [Source 2] |
|--------|----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Offence** | Voluntarily causing hurt in committing or attempting to commit robbery | Same: voluntarily causing hurt in committing or attempting to commit robbery |
| **Persons liable** | The offender and any other person jointly concerned | Same: the offender and any other person jointly concerned |
| **Punishment** | Imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine | Identical: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine |

---

**Key Observations**

1. **Structural difference** – In the IPC, the offence is a standalone section (Section 394). In the BNS, it is embedded as **sub-section (6) of Section 309**, which consolidates the definition, basic punishment, and aggravated forms of robbery in a single section.
2. **No substantive change** – The wording, scope of joint liability, and quantum of punishment are identical.
3. **Related aggravated provision** – BNS Section 311 [Source 3] prescribes a minimum 7‑year imprisonment when robbery/dacoity involves a deadly weapon, grievous hurt, or attempt to cause death/grievous hurt. This is a separate, higher‑threshold aggravation and does not replace Section 309(6).

**Practical Implication**  
Prosecutors and courts will now charge the offence under **BNS Section 309(6)** instead of IPC Section 394. The elements to prove, the range of punishment, and the principle of joint liability remain unchanged, so existing case law on IPC Section 394 continues to be directly applicable.

question: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 207 of the Indian Penal Code (Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution)?
expanded: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 207 of the Indian Penal Code (Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
Section 244 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 207 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Both provisions are titled “Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution” and contain substantially identical language and punishment.

---

**Statutory Text (Key Provisions)**  

| Provision | Text (excerpt) |
|-----------|----------------|
| **IPC Section 207** [Source 2] | “Whoever fraudulently accepts, receives or claims any property or any interest therein, knowing that he has no right or rightful claim to such property or interest, or practices any deception touching any right to any property or any interest therein, intending thereby to prevent that property or interest therein from being taken as a forfeiture or in satisfaction of a fine, under a sentence which has been pronounced, or which he knows to be likely to be pronounced by a **Court of Justice** or other competent authority, or from being taken in execution of a decree or order which has been made, or which he knows to be likely to be made by a **Court of Justice** in a civil suit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.” |
| **BNS Section 244** [Source 1] | “Whoever fraudulently accepts, receives or claims any property or any interest therein, knowing that he has no right or rightful claim to such property or interest, or practises any deception touching any right to any property or any interest therein, intending thereby to prevent that property or interest therein from being taken as a forfeiture or in satisfaction of a fine, under a sentence which has been pronounced, or which he knows to be likely to be pronounced by a **Court** or other competent authority, or from being taken in execution of a decree or order which has been made, or which he knows to be likely to be made by a **Court** in a civil suit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.” |

---

**Differences Between IPC and BNS (based on retrieved sources)**  

1. **Terminology** – IPC refers to “Court of Justice” twice; BNS shortens this to “Court” in both places.  
2. **Spelling** – IPC uses “practices”; BNS uses “practises” (British spelling).  
3. **Punishment** – Identical: imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.  
4. **Chapter Placement** – Both reside in the chapter on “False Evidence and Offences against Public Justice” (IPC Chapter XI, BNS Chapter XIV).

No substantive change in elements of the offence, mental state, or penalty is evident from the texts provided.

---

**Practical Implication**  
The correspondence is one-to-one: prosecutors, defence counsel, and courts can treat BNS Section 244 as the direct successor to IPC Section 207. Existing case law on Section 207 will remain relevant for interpreting the identical ingredients — fraudulent claim, knowledge of lack of right, intent to prevent seizure under judicial process — under the new provision.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY | Section 317: Stolen property
317. Stolen property.—(1) Property, the possession whereof has been transferred by theft or
extortion or robbery or cheating, and property which has been criminally misappropriated or in respect of
which criminal breach of trust has been committed, is designated as stolen property, whether the transfer
has been made, or the misappropriation or breach of trust has been committed, within or without India,
but, if such property subsequently comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to the possession
thereof, it then ceases to be stolen property.
(2) Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, knowing or having reason to believe
the same to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term
which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
(3) Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen property, the possession whereof he knows or
has reason to believe to have been transferred by the commission of dacoity, or dishonestly receives from
a person, whom he knows or has reason to believe to belong or to have belonged to a gang of dacoits,
property which he knows or has reason to believe to have been stolen, shall be punished with
imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall
also be liable to fine.
(4) Whoever habitually receives or deals in property which he knows or has reason to believe to be
stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description
for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(5) Whoever voluntarily assists in concealing or disposing of or making away with property which he
knows or has reason to believe to be stolen property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either
description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

question: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 311 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt)?

answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
The predecessor of BNS Section 311 is **IPC Section 397**. Both provisions carry the identical title and text: “Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt.” [Source 1] [Source 2]

**Statutory Text (identical in both Codes):**  
> “If, at the time of committing robbery or dacoity, the offender uses any deadly weapon, or causes grievous hurt to any person, or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt to any person, the imprisonment with which such offender shall be punished shall not be less than seven years.”  
> — IPC Section 397 [Source 2] / BNS Section 311 [Source 1]

| Aspect | IPC (1860) | BNS (2023) |
|--------|------------|------------|

| Chapter | Chapter XVII – Of Offences Against Property | Chapter XVII – Of Offences Against Property |
| Text | Identical | Identical |
| Minimum punishment | Not less than 7 years’ imprisonment | Not less than 7 years’ imprisonment |

**Practical Implications:**  
The provision has been renumbered (397 → 311) without any substantive change in language, elements, or minimum sentence. Practitioners should note the new section number for citations, pleadings, and charging documents under the BNS, but the legal test and sentencing floor remain exactly the same.

310. Dacoity.—(1) When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit a robbery, or
where the whole number of persons conjointly committing or attempting to commit a robbery, and
persons present and aiding such commission or attempt, amount to five or more, every person so
committing, attempting or aiding, is said to commit dacoity.
(2) Whoever commits dacoity shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous
imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(3) If any one of five or more persons, who are conjointly committing dacoity, commits murder in so
committing dacoity, every one of those persons shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, or
rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(4) Whoever makes any preparation for committing dacoity, shall be punished with rigorous
imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(5) Whoever is one of five or more persons assembled for the purpose of committing dacoity, shall be
punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable
to fine.
(6) Whoever belongs to a gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing
dacoity, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which
may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIV - OF FALSE EVIDENCE AND OFFENCES AGAINST PUBLIC JUSTICE | Section 254: Penalty for harbouring robbers or dacoits
254. Penalty for harbouring robbers or dacoits.—Whoever, knowing or having reason to believe
that any persons are about to commit or have recently committed robbery or dacoity, harbours them or
any of them, with the intention of facilitating the commission of such robbery or dacoity, or of screening
them or any of them from punishment, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which

intended to be committed, or has been committed, within or without India.
Exception.—The provisions of this section do not extend to the case in which the harbour is by the
spouse of the offender.

metadata.section_title: Robbery
metadata.chapter: CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY
metadata.hierarchy_path: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita > CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY > Section 309

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XVII - OF OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY | Section 309: Robbery
309. Robbery.—(1) In all robbery there is either theft or extortion.
(2) Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in
carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end
voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant
death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.
(3) Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of
the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant
hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear,
induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.
Explanation.—The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in
fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.
(a) A holds Z down, and fraudulently takes Z’s money and jewels from Z’s clothes, without Z’s
consent. Here A has committed theft, and, in order to the committing of that theft, has voluntarily caused
wrongful restraint to Z. A has therefore committed robbery.
(b) A meets Z on the high road, shows a pistol, and demands Z’s purse. Z, in consequence, surrenders
his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z by putting him in fear of instant hurt, and being at the
time of committing the extortion in his presence. A has therefore committed robbery.
(c) A meets Z and Z’s child on the high road. A takes the child, and threatens to fling it down a
precipice, unless Z delivers his purse. Z, in consequence, delivers his purse. Here A has extorted the
purse from Z, by causing Z to be in fear of instant hurt to the child who is there present. A has therefore
committed robbery on Z.
(d) A obtains property from Z by saying—“Your child is in the hands of my gang, and will be put to
death unless you send us ten thousand rupees”. This is extortion, and punishable as such; but it is not
robbery, unless Z is put in fear of the instant death of his child.
(4) Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may
extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway
between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.
(5) Whoever attempts to commit robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term
which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
(6) If any person, in committing or in attempting to commit robbery, voluntarily causes hurt, such
person, and any other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting to commit such robbery, shall
be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to
ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER III - GENERAL EXCEPTIONS | Section 41: When right of private defence of property extends to causing death
41. When right of private defence of property extends to causing death.—The right of private
defence of property extends, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing of
death or of any other harm to the wrong-doer, if the offence, the committing of which, or the attempting
to commit which, occasions the exercise of the right, be an offence of any of the descriptions hereinafter
enumerated, namely: —
(a) robbery;
(b) house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise;

not exercised.

question: Compare Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
expanded: Compare Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave provocation) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
Section 133 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 is the direct successor to Section 355 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860. Both provisions criminalise assault or criminal force used with the intention of dishonouring a person, absent grave and sudden provocation, and prescribe identical punishments.

**Statutory Text**  

| Provision | Text |
|-----------|------|
| **BNS Section 133** [Source 1] | “Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonour that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.” |
| **IPC Section 355** [Source 2] | “Whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any person, intending thereby to dishonor that person, otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.” |

**Comparison (IPC vs BNS)**  

- **Wording**: The two sections are verbatim identical, including the qualification “otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person”.  
- **Punishment**: Both prescribe imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both.  
- **Chapter Placement**: BNS places the offence in **Chapter VI (Offences Affecting the Human Body)**, while IPC placed it in **Chapter XVI (Offences Affecting the Human Body)** – a structural renumbering only.  
- **Cross-references**: BNS Section 133 operates alongside Section 131 (general assault/criminal force without provocation) and Section 136 (assault on grave provocation) [Sources 3, 4], mirroring the IPC’s scheme where Section 355 sat beside Sections 352 and 358. No substantive change in the relationship between these provisions is evident from the retrieved texts.

**Practical Implications**  
The offence remains unchanged in definition, ingredients, and penalty. Practitioners can treat BNS Section 133 as a direct renumbering of IPC Section 355; existing case law on “intent to dishonour”, “grave and sudden provocation”, and the quantum of punishment continues to apply without modification.

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER VI - OF OFFENCES AFFECTING THE HUMAN BODY | Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation
131. Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation.—Whoever
assaults or uses criminal force to any person otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by
that person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to
three months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.
Explanation 1.—Grave and sudden provocation will not mitigate the punishment for an offence under
this section,—
(a) if the provocation is sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse for the
offence; or
(b) if the provocation is given by anything done in obedience to the law, or by a public servant, in
the lawful exercise of the powers of such public servant; or
(c) if the provocation is given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private
defence.
Explanation 2.—Whether the provocation was grave and sudden enough to mitigate the offence, is a
question of fact.

question: How does Section 153 of the Indian Penal Code (Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
expanded: How does Section 153 of the Indian Penal Code (Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
The counterpart to IPC Section 153 under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is **BNS Section 192**. The two provisions are **textually identical** — same ingredients, same two-tier punishment structure, and no substantive change in language.

---

**Statutory Text (identical in both codes)**  

*IPC Section 153* [Source 1]  
> “Whoever malignantly, or wantonly, by doing anything which is illegal, gives provocation to any person intending or knowing it to be likely that such provocation will cause the offence of rioting to be committed, shall, if the offence of rioting be committed in consequence of such provocation, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both; and if the offence of rioting be not committed, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.”

*BNS Section 192* [Source 2]  
> “Whoever malignantly, or wantonly by doing anything which is illegal, gives provocation to any person intending or knowing it to be likely that such provocation will cause the offence of rioting to be committed, shall, if the offence of rioting be committed in consequence of such provocation, be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both; and if the offence of rioting be not committed, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.”

---

**Differences Between IPC and BNS (only for the sections in the sources)**  

| Aspect | IPC | BNS |
|--------|-----|-----|
| **Section number** | 153 | 192 |
| **Chapter** | Chapter VIII – Offences Against the Public Tranquillity | Chapter XI – Offences Against the Public Tranquillity |
| **Wording** | Identical (including punctuation) | Identical |
| **Punishment** | Identical two-tier scale | Identical two-tier scale |

No substantive amendment, addition, or omission appears in the retrieved texts.

---

**Practical Implications**  
- The offence, its mental element (“malignantly or wantonly”), the requirement of an illegal act, and the conditional punishment based on whether rioting actually occurs remain unchanged.  
- Practitioners can rely on existing IPC case law when interpreting BNS Section 192.  
- The only procedural adjustment is citing the new section number (192) and chapter (XI) in pleadings, charges, and judgments under the BNS.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIV - OF FALSE EVIDENCE AND OFFENCES AGAINST PUBLIC JUSTICE | Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence
230. Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence.—
(1) Whoever gives or fabricates false evidence, intending thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that
he will thereby cause, any person to be convicted of an offence which is capital by the law for the time
being in force in India shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a
term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to fifty thousand
rupees.
(2) If an innocent person be convicted and executed in consequence of false evidence referred to in
sub-section (1), the person who gives such false evidence shall be punished either with death or the
punishment specified in sub-section (1).

231. Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable
with imprisonment for life or imprisonment.—Whoever gives or fabricates false evidence intending
thereby to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause, any person to be convicted of an
offence which by the law for the time being in force in India is not capital, but punishable with
imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term of seven years or upwards, shall be punished as a
person convicted of that offence would be liable to be punished.
A gives false evidence before a Court, intending thereby to cause Z to be convicted of a dacoity. The
punishment of dacoity is imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to
ten years, with or without fine. A, therefore, is liable to imprisonment for life or imprisonment, with or
without fine.

metadata.section_title: Rioting

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XI - OF OFFENCES AGAINST THE PUBLIC TRANQUILLITY | Section 191: Rioting
191. Rioting.—(1) Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member
thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty
of the offence of rioting.
(2) Whoever is guilty of rioting, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term
which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
(3) Whoever is guilty of rioting, being armed with a deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a
weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for
a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both.

chunks.document:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER XIX - OF CRIMINAL INTIMIDATION, INSULT, ANNOYANCE, DEFAMATION, ETC. | Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief
353. Statements conducing to public mischief.—(1) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any
statement, false information, rumour, or report, including through electronic means—
(a) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, any officer, soldier, sailor or airman in the
Army, Navy or Air Force of India to mutiny or otherwise disregard or fail in his duty as such; or
(b) with intent to cause, or which is likely to cause, fear or alarm to the public, or to any section
of the public whereby any person may be induced to commit an offence against the State or against
the public tranquillity; or
(c) with intent to incite, or which is likely to incite, any class or community of persons to commit
any offence against any other class or community,
shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
(2) Whoever makes, publishes or circulates any statement or report containing false information,
rumour or alarming news, including through electronic means, with intent to create or promote, or which
is likely to create or promote, on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, caste or
community or any other ground whatsoever, feelings of enmity, hatred or ill will between different
religious, racial, language or regional groups or castes or communities, shall be punished with
imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
(3) Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (2) in any place of worship or in any
assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished
with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.
Exception.—It does not amount to an offence, within the meaning of this section, when the person
making, publishing or circulating any such statement, false information, rumour or report, has reasonable
grounds for believing that such statement, false information, rumour or report is true and makes,
publishes or circulates it in good faith and without any such intent as aforesaid.

question: How does Section 12 of the Indian Penal Code (“Public”) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
expanded: How does Section 12 of the Indian Penal Code (“Public”) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
IPC Section 12 defines “public” as including any class of the public or any community. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) does not contain a corresponding definition of “public” in the retrieved sources. The BNS uses the term in several offence provisions (e.g., public nuisance, affray, public servant) but the definitions section (Section 2) provided in the sources does not define it.

**Statutory Text**  
- **IPC Section 12**: “The word ‘public’ includes any class of the public or any community.” [Source 1]  
- **BNS Section 2 (Definitions)**: The retrieved excerpt lists 39 defined terms (act, animal, child, counterfeit, Court, death, dishonestly, document, fraudulently, etc.) but does not include a definition for “public.” [Source 2]

**Comparison (based only on retrieved sources)**  
- The IPC expressly defines “public” in a standalone section (Section 12).  
- The BNS definitions section (Section 2) in the retrieved text omits any definition of “public.”  
- The BNS employs the undefined term “public” in provisions such as:  
  - Section 270 (Public nuisance) – “injury, danger or annoyance to the public” [Source 3]  
  - Section 194 (Affray) – “fighting in a public place” [Source 4]  
  - Section 202 (Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade) – “public servant” [Source 5]  
- Because the BNS definition is absent from the sources, no textual comparison of the two definitions can be made.

**Practical Implication**  
In the absence of a statutory definition in the BNS, courts will likely interpret “public” by resort to judicial precedent, the General Clauses Act, or the ordinary meaning of the term, potentially aligning with the IPC’s inclusive formulation (“any class of the public or any community”) until the legislature or higher courts provide a BNS-specific construction.

illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in

204. Personating a public servant.—Whoever pretends to hold any particular office as a public
servant, knowing that he does not hold such office or falsely personates any other person holding such
office, and in such assumed character does or attempts to do any act under colour of such office, shall be
punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than six months but
which may extend to three years and with fine.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER II - OF PUNISHMENTS | Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement
12. Limit of solitary confinement.—In executing a sentence of solitary confinement, such
confinement shall in no case exceed fourteen days at a time, with intervals between the periods of solitary
confinement of not less duration than such periods; and when the imprisonment awarded shall exceed
three months, the solitary confinement shall not exceed seven days in any one month of the whole
imprisonment awarded, with intervals between the periods of solitary confinement of not less duration
than such periods.

question: Compare Section 271 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
expanded: Compare Section 271 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life) with the corresponding provision of the Indian Penal Code.
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
Section 271 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 and Section 269 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860 are **identical in wording, elements, and punishment**. The only formal differences are the section numbers and the chapter numbers under which they appear.

---

**Statutory Text (Key Provisions)**  

| Provision | Text | Source |
|-----------|------|--------|
| **BNS Section 271** | “Whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act which is, and which he knows or has reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.” | [Source 1] |
| **IPC Section 269** | “Whoever unlawfully or negligently does any act which is, and which he knows or has reason to believe to be, likely to spread the infection of any disease dangerous to life, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.” | [Source 2] |

---

**Differences Between BNS and IPC (for the compared sections)**  

| Aspect | BNS Section 271 | IPC Section 269 |
|--------|----------------|----------------|
| **Section Number** | 271 | 269 |
| **Chapter** | Chapter XV – “Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals” | Chapter XIV – “Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals” |
| **Enactment Year** | 2023 | 1860 |
| **Substantive Text** | **Identical** | **Identical** |
| **Punishment** | Imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both | Imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both |

No substantive change has been made to the offence of *negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life* in the transition from IPC to BNS.

---

**Practical Implications**  
- **Continuity of Law**: Investigations, prosecutions, and judicial precedents under IPC Section 269 apply directly to BNS Section 271 without reinterpretation.  
- **Case Law**: All existing Supreme Court and High Court rulings on IPC Section 269 (e.g., on “unlawfully or negligently”, “knows or has reason to believe”, “disease dangerous to life”) remain binding authority for BNS Section 271.  
- **Charging Practice**: Police and prosecutors need only update the section number in FIRs, charge-sheets, and court filings; the ingredients of the offence and the quantum of punishment are unchanged.  
- **Related Provision**: The corresponding *malignant* act offence (BNS Section 272 / IPC Section 270) is likewise identical in text and punishment (imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both) [Source 3, Source 4].

question: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 83 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage)?
expanded: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 83 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
The predecessor of **BNS Section 83** is **IPC Section 496**. Both provisions are titled “Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage” and contain identical language.

**Statutory Text (Key Provisions)**  

| Provision | Text |
|-----------|------|
| **IPC Section 496** [Source 2] | “Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.” |
| **BNS Section 83** [Source 1] | “Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.” |

**Comparison (IPC vs. BNS)**  
- **Wording:** Identical — no substantive change in the definition, mental element (*dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention*), knowledge requirement (*knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married*), or punishment (*imprisonment up to seven years and fine*).  
- **Chapter Placement:** IPC Section 496 was in Chapter XX (Offences Relating to Marriage); BNS Section 83 is in Chapter V (Offences Against Woman and Child).  
- **Section Number:** Changed from 496 (IPC) to 83 (BNS).

**Practical Implications**  
- The offence remains unchanged in substance; existing case law under IPC Section 496 continues to apply.  
- The relocation to a chapter focused on offences against women and children may influence procedural treatment (e.g., special courts, victim‑protection measures) but does not alter the elements of the offence.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER V - OF OFFENCES AGAINST WOMAN AND CHILD | Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife
82. Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife.—(1) Whoever, having a husband or wife
living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of
such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may
extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
Exception.—This sub-section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or
wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction, nor to any person who contracts a
marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the
subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years,
and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person
contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with
whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her
knowledge.
(2) Whoever commits the offence under sub-section (1) having concealed from the person with
whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with
imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to
fine.

question: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita now punishes murder formerly punished under Section 302 IPC?
expanded: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita now punishes murder formerly punished under Section 302 IPC?
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
Murder formerly punished under **Section 302 IPC** is now punished under **Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023** [Source 1; Source 2].

---

**Statutory Text**

| Provision | Text |
|-----------|------|
| **IPC Section 302** | “Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.” [Source 2] |
| **BNS Section 103** | “(1) Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. (2) When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.” [Source 1] |

---

**Key Differences (based on the retrieved sources)**

1. **Group‑murder aggravation** – BNS Section 103(2) introduces a specific enhanced punishment for murder committed by a group of five or more persons acting in concert on enumerated discriminatory grounds (race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief, or similar). IPC Section 302 contains no such provision.  
2. **Structure** – BNS splits the offence into two sub‑sections (general murder and group‑based murder), whereas IPC Section 302 is a single provision.  
3. **Punishment quantum** – Both retain the same maximum penalties (death or imprisonment for life plus fine) for ordinary murder.

---

**Practical Implications**

- Prosecutors must now consider whether the facts attract BNS Section 103(2) for group‑based hate‑motivated murders, which carries the same penalty range but signals a distinct legislative focus on collective discriminatory violence.  
- Defence counsel should verify the charging section: ordinary murder charges will cite BNS Section 103(1), while group‑based allegations will invoke Section 103(2).  
- The corresponding provision for murder by a life‑convict (formerly IPC Section 303) is now **BNS Section 104** [Source 3], but that is a separate offence and not a replacement for Section 302.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 | CHAPTER VI - OF OFFENCES AFFECTING THE HUMAN BODY | Section 109: Attempt to murder
109. Attempt to murder.—(1) Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under
such circumstances that, if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder, shall be punished
with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable
to fine; and if hurt is caused to any person by such act, the offender shall be liable either to imprisonment
for life, or to such punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned.
(2) When any person offending under sub-section (1) is under sentence of imprisonment for life, he
may, if hurt is caused, be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the
remainder of that person’s natural life.
(a) A shoots at Z with intention to kill him, under such circumstances that, if death ensued, A would
be guilty of murder. A is liable to punishment under this section.
(b) A, with the intention of causing the death of a child of tender years, exposes it in a desert place. A
has committed the offence defined by this section, though the death of the child does not ensue.
(c) A, intending to murder Z, buys a gun and loads it. A has not yet committed the offence. A fires
the gun at Z. He has committed the offence defined in this section, and, if by such firing he wounds Z, he
is liable to the punishment provided by the latter part of sub-section (1).
(d) A, intending to murder Z by poison, purchases poison and mixes the same with food which
remains in A’s keeping; A has not yet committed the offence defined in this section. A places the food on
Z’s table or delivers it to Z’s servants to place it on Z’s table. A has committed the offence defined in this
section.

question: How does Section 489E of the Indian Penal Code (Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
expanded: How does Section 489E of the Indian Penal Code (Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes) compare with its counterpart under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
answer:
**Direct Answer**  
Section 489E of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 182 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) both criminalise the making, use, or delivery of documents that resemble currency‑notes or bank‑notes, and both contain a presumption linking a person whose name appears on such a document to its creation. The BNS provision increases the maximum fines: from ₹100 to ₹300 for the primary offence (sub‑section 1) and from ₹200 to ₹600 for refusing to disclose the printer’s details (sub‑section 2) [Source 1] [Source 2].

**Statutory Text – Key Provisions**  

| Provision | IPC Section 489E [Source 1] | BNS Section 182 [Source 2] |
|-----------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Sub‑section (1)** | “Whoever makes, or causes to be made, or uses for any purpose whatsoever, or delivers to any person, any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency‑note or bank‑note shall be punished with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees.” | Identical wording, but “shall be punished with fine which may extend to three hundred rupees.” |
| **Sub‑section (2)** | “If any person, whose name appears on a document the making of which is an offence under sub‑section (1), refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police‑officer on being so required the name and address of the person by whom it was printed or otherwise made, he shall be punished with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees.” | Same wording, except “police officer” (no hyphen) and “fine which may extend to six hundred rupees.” |
| **Sub‑section (3)** | “Where the name of any person appears on any document in respect of which any person is charged with an offence under sub‑section (1) or on any other document used or distributed in connection with that document it may, until the contrary is proved, be presumed that that person caused the document to be made.” | Identical, except “the person” replaces “that person.” |

**Differences Between IPC and BNS (Only for Sections Present in Sources)**  

1. **Fine amounts** – BNS triples the maximum fine for the main offence (₹100 → ₹300) and triples the fine for non‑disclosure (₹200 → ₹600) [Source 1] [Source 2].  
2. **Terminology** – “police‑officer” (IPC) becomes “police officer” (BNS); “that person” becomes “the person” in the presumption clause [Source 1] [Source 2].  
3. **Structure and language** – The substantive elements (acts prohibited, presumption) remain unchanged; only the quantum of fine and minor drafting updates differ.

**Practical Implications**  
The enhanced fines under BNS Section 182 reflect a legislative intent to strengthen deterrence against the circulation of deceptive currency‑like documents, adjusting for inflation and the greater economic impact of such offences. The unchanged presumption in sub‑section (3) continues to place an evidential burden on the person whose name appears on the document. No new offence categories or procedural changes are introduced in the counterpart provision.

**Direct Answer**  
Section 489E of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 182 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) both criminalise the making, use, or delivery of documents that resemble currency‑notes or bank‑notes, and both contain a presumption linking a person whose name appears on such a document to its creation. The BNS provision increases the maximum fines: from ₹100 to ₹300 for the primary offence (sub‑section 1) and from ₹200 to ₹600 for refusing to disclose the printer’s details (sub‑section 2) [Source 1] [Source 2].

**Statutory Text – Key Provisions**  

| Provision | IPC Section 489E [Source 1] | BNS Section 182 [Source 2] |
|-----------|-----------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Sub‑section (1)** | “Whoever makes, or causes to be made, or uses for any purpose whatsoever, or delivers to any person, any document purporting to be, or in any way resembling, or so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive, any currency‑note or bank‑note shall be punished with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees.” | Identical wording, but “shall be punished with fine which may extend to three hundred rupees.” |
| **Sub‑section (2)** | “If any person, whose name appears on a document the making of which is an offence under sub‑section (1), refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police‑officer on being so required the name and address of the person by whom it was printed or otherwise made, he shall be punished with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees.” | Same wording, except “police officer” (no hyphen) and “fine which may extend to six hundred rupees.” |
| **Sub‑section (3)** | “Where the name of any person appears on any document in respect of which any person is charged with an offence under sub‑section (1) or on any other document used or distributed in connection with that document it may, until the contrary is proved, be presumed that that person caused the document to be made.” | Identical, except “the person” replaces “that person.” |

**Differences Between IPC and BNS (Only for Sections Present in Sources)**  

1. **Fine amounts** – BNS triples the maximum fine for the main offence (₹100 → ₹300) and triples the fine for non‑disclosure (₹200 → ₹600) [Source 1] [Source 2].  
2. **Terminology** – “police‑officer” (IPC) becomes “police officer” (BNS); “that person” becomes “the person” in the presumption clause [Source 1] [Source 2].  
3. **Structure and language** – The substantive elements (acts prohibited, presumption) remain unchanged; only the quantum of fine and minor drafting updates differ.

**Practical Implications**  
The enhanced fines under BNS Section 182 reflect a legislative intent to strengthen deterrence against the circulation of deceptive currency‑like documents, adjusting for inflation and the greater economic impact of such offences. The unchanged presumption in sub‑section (3) continues to place an evidential burden on the person whose name appears on the document. question: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 160 of the Indian Penal Code (Punishment for committing affray)?
expanded: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 160 of the Indian Penal Code (Punishment for committing affray)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
Section 194 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) corresponds to Section 160 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC). Both deal with the offence of affray and its punishment.

---

**Statutory Text**

| Provision | Text |
|-----------|------|
| **IPC Section 160** | “Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one hundred rupees, or with both.” [Source 2] |
| **BNS Section 194** | “(1) When two or more persons, by fighting in a public place, disturb the public peace, they are said to commit an affray. (2) Whoever commits an affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.” [Source 1] |

---

**Key Differences (based on retrieved sources)**

1. **Structure** – BNS Section 194 combines the definition of affray (sub‑section 1) and the punishment (sub‑section 2) in a single section, whereas the IPC places the definition in Section 159 and the punishment in Section 160.
2. **Fine Amount** – The maximum fine is raised from **₹100 (IPC)** to **₹1,000 (BNS)**.
3. **Imprisonment Term** – Identical: up to one month, of either description.
4. **Section Number** – The offence of affray moves from **IPC Section 160** to **BNS Section 194**; BNS Section 160 deals with an entirely different offence (abetment of mutiny) [Source 4].

---

**Practical Implication**  
The substantive ingredients of the offence remain unchanged, but the tenfold increase in the maximum fine reflects the BNS’s general trend of updating monetary penalties. Prosecutors and courts will apply BNS Section 194 for any affray committed after the Sanhita’s commencement, and the higher fine ceiling may be invoked where the circumstances warrant.

question: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 346 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Tampering with property mark with intent to cause injury)?
expanded: Which section of the Indian Penal Code is the predecessor of Section 346 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (Tampering with property mark with intent to cause injury)?
answer:
**Direct Answer:**  
The predecessor of BNS Section 346 (Tampering with property mark with intent to cause injury) is **IPC Section 489**.

**Statutory Text Comparison**  

| Provision | Text |
|-----------|------|
| **IPC Section 489** [Source 2] | “Whoever removes, destroys, defaces or adds to any property mark, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.” |
| **BNS Section 346** [Source 1] | “Whoever removes, destroys, defaces or adds to any property mark, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury to any person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.” |

**Differences Between IPC and BNS**  
- **Section number changed** from 489 (IPC) to 346 (BNS).  
- **Substantive text is identical** — no change in definition, mental element, or punishment.  
- **Chapter placement**: both remain in Chapter XVIII (Offences Relating to Documents and to Property Marks).

**Practical Implication**  
The renumbering is purely structural; the offence, its ingredients, and the maximum penalty (one year’s imprisonment, fine, or both) remain unchanged. Practitioners can rely on existing IPC Section 489 case law when interpreting BNS Section 346.

other person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to
two years, or with fine, or with both.

326. Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.—Whoever commits
mischief by,—
(a) doing any act which causes, or which he knows to be likely to cause, a diminution of the
supply of water for agricultural purposes, or for food or drink for human beings or for animals which
are property, or for cleanliness or for carrying on any manufacture, shall be punished with
imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with
both;
(b) doing any act which renders or which he knows to be likely to render any public road, bridge,
navigable river or navigable channel, natural or artificial, impassable or less safe for travelling or
conveying property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may
extend to five years, or with fine, or with both;
(c) doing any act which causes or which he knows to be likely to cause an inundation or an
obstruction to any public drainage attended with injury or damage, shall be punished with
imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with
both;
(d) destroying or moving any sign or signal used for navigation of rail, aircraft or ship or other
thing placed as a guide for navigators, or by any act which renders any such sign or signal less useful
as a guide for navigators, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which
may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both;
(e) destroying or moving any land-mark fixed by the authority of a public servant, or by any act
which renders such land-mark less useful as such, shall be punished with imprisonment of either
description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both;
(f) fire or any explosive substance intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will
thereby cause, damage to any property including agricultural produce, shall be punished with
imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be
liable to fine;
(g) fire or any explosive substance, intending to cause, or knowing it to be likely that he will
thereby cause, the destruction of any building which is ordinarily used as a place of worship or as a
human dwelling or as a place for the custody of property, shall be punished with imprisonment for
life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall
also be liable to fine.
